From a DC source to a controlled AC voltage

  1. Build the voltage.
    H-bridge states and safe switching.
  2. Choose the switching pattern.
    Square wave and phase shift.
  3. Improve the waveform.
    Bipolar and unipolar sinusoidal PWM.

How do we control the fundamental and manage the harmonics?

The H-bridge: two legs, one output

N: voltage reference.

Leg A: S1 / S3
Leg B: S2 / S4

Each leg connects its pole to one dc rail: \(v_{AN},v_{BN}\in\{0,v_d\}\).

\(v_t=v_{AN}-v_{BN}\)

Four switch states, three voltage levels

In each commanded state, one switch per leg is on.

Prevent shoot-through

Shoot-through: the leg directly shorts the DC source.

The same rule applies to the other leg.

How do we transition between the upper and lower switches without overlap?

Dead time prevents overlap

1. Turn off \(S_1\).

2. Wait.

3. Turn on \(S_3\).

A current source must keep a current path

Overlap time keeps a current path

1. Turn on \(S_3\).

2. Wait.

3. Turn off \(S_1\).

Modulation

Switch modulation: the strategy that generates the gate signals for a converter’s switches.

Square Wave: Gate Pattern

For \(x\in\{1,\ldots,4\}\): \(S_x=1\) means ON and \(S_x=0\) means OFF; \(\overline{S}_x=0\) means ON and \(\overline{S}_x=1\) means OFF.
Each gate is ON for \(0.5T_1\). The \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) gate patterns are shifted by \(0.5T_1\).

Square Wave: Phase Relative to a Reference

reference switched vt fundamental: V̂t,1 = 4vd/π peak

For square-wave operation, phase is the only control variable. The square wave and its fundamental shift together; the fundamental peak stays fixed at \(4v_d/\pi\).

Square Wave: Harmonics

\(\displaystyle \hat V_{t,k}=\frac{4v_{d}}{k\pi},\quad k=1,3,5,\ldots\) (peak); even harmonics are zero. Voltage THD \(=48.3\%\).

Phase Shift: Gate Pattern

Each gate is ON for \(0.5T_1\). The zero interval is \(\alpha T_1\).
\(0\leq\alpha\leq0.5\).

Phase Shift: Effect of the Shift

V̂t,1 = 0.900 vd peak · THDv = 48.3% · bk < 0

Example: low-order harmonic currents

Square-wave bridge: \(v_d=400\,\mathrm{Vdc}\), \(\omega_1=377\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), and \(L=10\,\mathrm{mH}\).

\(\hat V_{t,k}=4v_d/(\pi k)\) and \(|\underline Z_{L,k}|=k\omega_1L\), so \(\hat I_{t,k}=\hat V_{t,k}/(k\omega_1L)\).

k \(\hat V_{t,k}\) (V) \(k\omega_1L\) (Ω) \(\hat I_{t,k}\) (A peak)
3 169.8 11.31 15.01
5 101.9 18.85 5.40
7 72.8 26.39 2.76

Move the harmonics to higher frequencies.

Bipolar PWM: Duty Sets the Average

Let \(d\) be the fraction of the switching period \(T_s=1/f_{sw}\) spent at \(+v_d\): \(0\le d\le1\).

\(\displaystyle \langle v_t\rangle_{T_s}=\frac{dT_s(+v_d)+(1-d)T_s(-v_d)}{T_s}=(2d-1)v_d\).

Period \(k\) is centred at \(t_k\): \(\displaystyle d_k=\frac{1+m_i\sin(\omega_1t_k)}{2}\), modulation index \(0\le m_i\le1\).

Each step: \(\langle v_t\rangle_{T_s,k}=(2d_k-1)v_d=m_iv_d\sin(\omega_1t_k)\).

\(f_{sw}\gg f_1\): staircase \(\approx m_iv_d\sin(\omega_1t)\) \(\Rightarrow\hat V_{t,1}\approx m_iv_d\).

How Do We Generate the Bipolar PWM Switching Waveform?

\(m_f=f_{sw}/f_1\) (frequency modulation ratio): the number of switching periods per fundamental period. A larger \(m_f\) makes the carrier-cycle average track the sinusoid more closely.

Building the Bipolar PWM Waveform

Choosing the Modulation Command

Want \(\hat V_{t,1}=340\,\mathrm{V}\) from \(v_{d}=425\,\mathrm{V}\). What do we command?

Sinusoidal PWM (linear, \(m_i\le1\)): \(\hat V_{t,1}=m_iv_{d}\Rightarrow m_i=340/425=0.800\).

Phase shift: \(\hat V_{t,1}=\dfrac{4v_{d}}{\pi}\cos(\pi\alpha)\Rightarrow\cos(\pi\alpha)=\dfrac{340\pi}{4(425)}=0.628\), \(\alpha=0.284\).

Square wave: \(\hat V_{t,1}=4v_{d}/\pi\) is fixed, so the bus must change: \(v_{d}=340\pi/4=267\,\mathrm{V}\).

Bipolar PWM: Harmonic Spectrum

\(m_f=f_{sw}/f_1\) (frequency modulation ratio). Order \(h\) means \(hf_1\), so \(m_f\) marks \(f_{sw}\), \(2m_f\) marks \(2f_{sw}\), and so on. Example: \(m_i=0.8\). Magnitudes vary with \(m_i\); frequencies do not.

Reading the Harmonic Table

ch = V̂t,h/vd: the normalized amplitude of harmonic h, so V̂t,h = chvd for any dc voltage (bipolar full bridge). Each ± row gives the magnitude of each sideband.

Example: row \(2m_f\pm3\) holds \(h=2m_f-3\), at \((2m_f-3)f_1=2f_{sw}-3f_1\). If \(f_1=60\,\mathrm{Hz}\) and \(f_{sw}=2340\,\mathrm{Hz}\): \(2(2340)-3(60)=4500\,\mathrm{Hz}\), peak \(0.139\,v_d\) at \(m_i=0.8\).

Overmodulation: Back Toward the Square Wave

Table 8-1 assumes \(m_i\le1\) (linear range): \(\hat V_{t,1}=m_iv_d\).

\(m_i>1\): near the peaks the reference clears the carrier, so pulses drop out. \(\hat V_{t,1}\) grows less than linearly and low-order harmonics return.

\(m_i\) \(\hat V_{t,1}/v_d\) \(\hat V_{t,3}/v_d\)
0.8 0.80 0
1.5 1.17 0.17
2.5 1.24 0.34
\(\to\infty\) \(4/\pi=1.27\) 0.42

Limit: the square wave. Overmodulation trades waveform quality for at most 27% more fundamental.

\(m_f\): modern converters run \(m_f\gg21\), so its exact value hardly matters. Low-\(m_f\) rules: Mohan §8-2-1.

Worked Example: PWM Harmonic Current

Bipolar SPWM: \(v_d=525\,\mathrm{Vdc}\)

\(\hat V_{t,1}=509.3\,\mathrm{V}\), \(f_1=60\,\mathrm{Hz}\)

\(f_{sw}=2700\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(L=10\,\mathrm{mH}\)

Find \(\hat I_{t,h}\) of the lowest harmonic.

Same fundamental: square wave \(15.0\,\mathrm{A}\) at \(k=3\); PWM \(0.98\,\mathrm{A}\) at \(h=43\).

\(m_f=f_{sw}/f_1=2700/60=45\)

Which harmonic comes first? \(h=m_f-2=43\), at \(2580\,\mathrm{Hz}\) (row \(m_f\pm2\))

\(m_i=\hat V_{t,1}/v_d=509.3/525=0.9701\)

lower entry target upper entry
mi 0.800 0.9701 1.000
\(c_h\) 0.220 0.3033 0.318

\(\displaystyle c_h=0.220+\frac{0.9701-0.800}{1.000-0.800}(0.318-0.220)=0.3033\)

\(\hat V_{t,h}=c_hv_d=0.3033(525)=159.2\,\mathrm{V}\)

\(\hat I_{t,h}=\hat V_{t,h}/(2\pi hf_1L)=159.2/[2\pi(43)(60)(0.010)]=159.2/162.1=0.982\,\mathrm{A}\)

Bipolar’s Remaining Problem

Bipolar SPWM already pushed the harmonics up around \(m_f=45\): the lowest sits at \(h=43\) (2580 Hz, \(0.98\,\mathrm{A}\)), but the carrier harmonic itself is bigger: \(\hat V_{t,45}=c_{45}v_d=0.6334(525)=332.6\,\mathrm{V}\) at 2700 Hz.

\(\hat I_{t,45}=332.6/[2\pi(45)(60)(0.010)]=332.6/169.6=1.96\,\mathrm{A}\). Much smaller than the square wave’s third harmonic, but still the load’s largest PWM harmonic.

Same fundamental and same \(v_{d}\). Can the first harmonic group move out to \(2m_f\) without switching faster?

Building the Unipolar PWM Waveform

Notice: each switch still turns on and off only once per carrier cycle, yet \(v_t\) changes level twice as often: its effective switching frequency is \(2f_{sw}\).

Unipolar PWM: Harmonic Spectrum

The \(m_f\) group cancels; the first surviving group sits at \(2m_f\pm1\), around the effective \(2f_{sw}\) from the previous slide.

Unipolar SPWM, same bridge: \(v_d=525\,\mathrm{Vdc}\)

\(\hat V_{t,1}=509.3\,\mathrm{V}\), \(f_1=60\,\mathrm{Hz}\)

\(f_{sw}=2700\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(L=10\,\mathrm{mH}\)

Find \(\hat I_{t,h}\) of the first group.

Bipolar’s largest: \(1.96\,\mathrm{A}\) at \(h=45\). Unipolar: \(0.31\,\mathrm{A}\), six times less.

\(m_f=f_{sw}/f_1=2700/60=45\) (same as bipolar)

Which group comes first? The \(m_f\) rows cancel: \(h=2m_f-1=89\), at \(5340\,\mathrm{Hz}\) (row \(2m_f\pm1\))

\(m_i=\hat V_{t,1}/v_d=509.3/525=0.9701\) (unchanged)

lower entry target upper entry
mi 0.800 0.9701 1.000
\(c_h\) 0.314 0.2009 0.181

\(\displaystyle c_h=0.314+\frac{0.9701-0.800}{1.000-0.800}(0.181-0.314)=0.2009\)

\(\hat V_{t,h}=c_hv_d=0.2009(525)=105.5\,\mathrm{V}\)

\(\hat I_{t,h}=\hat V_{t,h}/(2\pi hf_1L)=105.5/[2\pi(89)(60)(0.010)]=105.5/335.5=0.314\,\mathrm{A}\)
